# ViLM Plugin Architecture

> Umbrella specification for a plugin architecture in ViLM: a plugin registry, a Settings screen for installing and configuring plugins, and a shared enrichment review pipeline that every plugin feeds. Individual plugins are specified on their own pages. **Status: Draft — awaiting Human Operator approval. No code may be written until Status = Approved.**
## Intention
ViLM's catalogue is enriched by hand. Several external sources could fill it automatically, but each carries its own vocabulary, licence, credential and appropriateness, and baking any one of them into the app makes the app about that source.
The architecture keeps the core generic. **Core owns the schema, the merge policy, and the review UI. A plugin owns exactly one thing: how to turn a name or a title into candidate records from one source.** No plugin writes to the library. It proposes; core decides how the proposal is reviewed and applied.
The architecture is the deliverable. Any individual plugin is replaceable.
## D1 — Distribution: personal builds, not the App Store
**Decision (Human Operator).** ViLM is built and installed personally. It is not distributed through the App Store.
This removes the constraint that shaped the first draft. App Store review requires an app to be self-contained and forbids downloading code that changes features, which would have forced plugins to be declarative manifests — JSON describing endpoints, auth, query shape and field mappings — interpreted at runtime by a generic engine. That engine is no longer necessary.
**Consequence.** A plugin is ordinary Swift, compiled into the build. The design problem is no longer *how to ship code that cannot be shipped* but *how the core stays ignorant of any particular source*.
⚠️ Revisit if App Store distribution ever becomes a goal. The manifest-interpreter design is the fallback and is materially more work.
## D2 — A plugin is a Swift package, linked at build time
Each plugin is a Swift package depending on `LibraryCore` and nothing else. The app target links the packages the operator wants available.
Registration happens in an **untracked local file**, so the public repository names no plugin at all and the app target compiles identically whether any package is present or absent:
```swift
// PluginBootstrap.swift — tracked, public. Names no plugin.
enum PluginBootstrap {
    static func registerAll(into registry: PluginRegistry) {
        #if LOCAL_PLUGINS
        registry.registerLocalPlugins()   // LocalPlugins.swift — untracked
        #endif
    }
}
```
`LocalPlugins.swift` is gitignored, and `LOCAL_PLUGINS` is set in an untracked xcconfig. **The public repository therefore contains the extension point and nothing that uses it** — no module name, no package reference, no evidence of which plugins exist. The earlier `#if canImport(<module>)` sketch is superseded: it required the public app target to name each module, which publishes the plugin roster.
Package dependency wiring is likewise untracked. A local path dependency committed to `Package.swift` or the project file would publish a plugin's existence and its path just as effectively as an import statement.
## D3 — Available, installed, enabled
Three states collapse to two the user can see.
| State | Meaning | Set by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Available | The package is linked into this build | Build configuration |
| Installed | The operator enabled it and supplied any credential | Settings |
**Nothing installs by default.** Every available plugin ships disabled, unconfigured, and inert. Before installation a plugin has no UI affordance anywhere in the app and issues **no network request of any kind**. This is asserted by test (T3), not by inspection.
Uninstalling clears the credential from Keychain and purges that plugin's response cache.
## D4 — The core contract
Core declares the protocols. It declares no source.
- `Plugin` — identity and description: `id`, `displayName`, `summary`, `capabilities`, `credentialRequirement` (`none` / `apiKey` / `token`), `attribution`, `homepage`.
- `VideoMetadataProvider` — `search(title:year:)` → candidates; `fetch(id:)` → `VideoMetadataProposal`; `artwork(id:)` → artwork references.
- `ActorMetadataProvider` — `search(name:)` → candidates; `fetch(id:)` → `ActorMetadataProposal`.
A plugin declares which provider protocols it implements; one plugin may implement both. The proposal types are core's canonical vocabulary. **A plugin never returns its source's enums** — mapping into ViLM's vocabulary happens inside the plugin, which is where source-specific knowledge belongs.
### Acceptance criteria
- `LibraryCore` and the app target contain no endpoint URL, no source name, and no source-specific enum.
- Adding a second plugin requires zero changes to core. If it doesn't, the abstraction has failed.
- With every plugin package removed, the app compiles and all existing features work.
## D5 — The merge policy belongs to core, not to plugins
The non-destructive rules already worked out for the first provider are generic, and promoting them into core is the highest-value part of this epic.
- **Fills** — target blank, source has a value. Safe to apply.
- **Conflicts** — target and source disagree. **Never auto-applied.** Presented for review.
- **Unchanged** — agreement, or no source data.
A blank source value never clears a populated target. Tags, gallery URLs and AKAs are preserved. Curated artwork is never silently replaced.
**Every plugin routes through one review sheet.** The user sees a field-by-field diff — current value, proposed value, source — and confirms before anything is written. Writing this once means it is tested once and cannot be circumvented by a badly behaved plugin, because plugins have no write path at all.
## D6 — Credentials, caching and rate limits are core services
- **Keychain.** Credentials are stored per plugin id, never in `UserDefaults`, never in a repository, never in a build.
- **Shared HTTP client.** Core provides it, with per-plugin rate-limit configuration declared by the plugin.
- **Response cache.** On disk, keyed by plugin id plus request hash. Enables offline replay and keeps tests network-free. Purged on uninstall.
## D7 — One repository per plugin, private by default
The compile-time feature flag in the earlier design is superseded. **A package's absence from the dependency graph is the gate** — stronger than a flag, and it needs no build configuration.
**Decision (Human Operator).** **Every plugin lives in its own repository, and every plugin repository is private.** No plugin package lives in the ViLM repository, regardless of how innocuous its source is.
**ViLM itself will be open source.** The plugin architecture — registry, protocols, merge engine, review sheet, Settings screen — is part of that public codebase and is the interesting work. The plugins are not released, and releasing them is not currently under consideration (see D9).
|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| One repo per plugin | A plugin is an independent unit with its own source, licence obligations, credential, release cadence and risk profile. Bundling two into one repository couples decisions that have no reason to be coupled. |
| Private by default | Created with `--private`, explicitly, and visibility **verified after creation, not assumed**. Never created public "for now" — a public repository is cloned, cached and indexed within minutes, and flipping to private retracts nothing. |
| Never referenced from public history | No branch name, commit message, PR title, issue or dependency entry in the public ViLM repository names a plugin, its source, or its module. |
**Plugin specifications live with their code**, on pages carrying `Repo = other` and syncing into the plugin's own repository. A detailed spec published in the public ViLM repository would announce a roster that is deliberately unpublished.
### Naming convention — capability, never source
**Decision (Human Operator).** Repositories and modules are named for **what the plugin enriches**, never for where it gets the data.
| Repository | Module | Enriches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `vilm-plugin-video-metadata` | `VilmPluginVideoMetadata` | Videos |
| `vilm-plugin-actor-metadata` | `VilmPluginActorMetadata` | Actors |
| `vilm-plugin-actor-video-metadata` | `VilmPluginActorVideoMetadata` | Both |
The point is **uniformity**, not secrecy. A scheme where every repository names its source except one makes that one conspicuous; a scheme where none of them does makes them all unremarkable. Applied consistently, no plugin stands out, and the third repository reads as the combined-capability one rather than as the odd one.
⚠️ **What this does and does not buy.** It protects against a glance at a repository list — a future collaborator, a backup service, an account audit. It does nothing against anyone who opens the code, where the endpoint is on the first screen. The naming convention is not a substitute for keeping the repositories private.
❓ **Known collision.** The convention allows one implementation per capability and no room for a second. A second video source cannot also be `vilm-plugin-video-metadata`, and resolving that by appending the source name to the newcomer would **reintroduce exactly the asymmetry this convention removes** — the older repository generic, the newer one named. Revisit the whole scheme at that point rather than patching it. Not a live problem with three plugins.
**In-app display names are a separate surface** and are not bound by this. They appear only on the operator's device, and a source carrying an attribution requirement must be named there regardless of what its repository is called.
⚠️ **Publication discipline.** Any Notion page with `Repo = ViLM` is a publication channel into a public repository. **This page is the only one in this epic that carries it.** Every plugin spec carries `Repo = other`, and none is named or linked from here.
## D8 — Privacy posture
Installing a plugin means titles or names leave the device. That is a real change and the install sheet states it plainly, once, at install time — what is sent, to whom, and whether the request is anonymous or attributable to an account.
Uninstalled, the app performs no plugin network I/O. Pre-existing image loading is unaffected and unrelated.
`PRIVACY.md` and the application charter currently describe the app as offline and zero-network, which is already inaccurate today because profile images download automatically. **This epic depends on that correction landing** — not as a blocker for design, but because shipping plugins on top of an inaccurate privacy statement compounds the problem.
## D9 — Local-only is the principle; a plugin is a deliberate exception to it
**Decision (Human Operator).** ViLM's core principle is local-only operation. **Plugins are the mechanism by which that principle can be knowingly broken** — per plugin, per install, per action.
This is why the plugins stay unreleased. Shipping the architecture publicly is safe: an unconfigured ViLM with no plugin packages linked behaves exactly as it does today. Shipping plugins publicly would make online operation a normal, expected part of what ViLM is, and **that shift deserves considerably more thought than it has had.** Open questions it raises — what a user reasonably expects when they install one, what the privacy documentation must then say, whether a plugin can be trusted not to exfiltrate, how a third party's plugin would ever be reviewed — are not answered here and do not need to be, because nothing is being released.
**Consequences for this epic:**
- The default build — the one the public repository produces — links no plugin and is fully local-only. This is the shipped configuration.
- Nothing in the public codebase advertises, documents by name, or provides a discovery mechanism for plugins. The extension point is documented; the roster is not.
- Third-party plugin support is **explicitly out of scope.** No plugin manifest format, no directory, no sideload path.
- If plugins are ever released, that is a separate decision requiring its own spec. This epic does not authorise it and should not be read as a step toward it.
## Plugin inventory
| Plugin | Enriches | Credential | Spec |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Video Metadata | Videos | API key | Separate private repo; page `Repo = other` |
| Actor Metadata | Actors | None | Separate private repo; page `Repo = other` |
| Actor & Video Metadata | Actors and videos | API key | Separate private repo and page, `Repo = other` — source not named here per D7 |
## Settings — Plugins screen
Settings → **Plugins**. A list of available plugins, each row showing name, one-line summary, and state.
Plugin detail shows: what it enriches, where the data comes from, the licence and any required attribution, what credential it needs, and an Install / Remove control. Once installed it also shows last-used time and a cache-size line with a purge control.
When no packages are linked: *No plugins are available in this build.* Not an error, not a prompt to go find some.
### Where enrichment appears
An installed plugin adds an **Enrich** action to Video Details and to Edit Actor Profile, matched to its capabilities. With one installed plugin for that entity type the action goes straight to search; with several it opens a source picker first. With none installed the action is **absent** — not disabled, not hidden in a menu.
## Delivery phases
1. **Registry and contract.** `Plugin`, the two provider protocols, `PluginRegistry`, `PluginBootstrap`. No plugins, no UI. Shippable and inert.
2. **Merge and review.** The three-way diff engine and the review sheet, driven by a test double provider.
3. **Settings screen.** Install / uninstall, Keychain credential entry, cache controls.
4. **First plugin.** A video metadata provider — proves the abstraction against a real source.
5. **Second plugin.** An actor metadata provider — proves it a second time. If phase 5 requires changes to phases 1–3, record what and why; that is the real test of D4.
## Test strategy
- **T1 — No-plugin build.** With all packages removed the app compiles, tests pass, every existing feature works.
- **T2 — Core is source-agnostic.** Grepping core and the app target for endpoint URLs or source names returns zero hits.
- **T3 — Uninstalled means inert.** No UI affordance, no credential prompt, and zero outbound requests from an uninstalled plugin.
- **T4 — Non-destructive merge.** A blank proposal never clears a populated field. Tags, AKAs, gallery URLs and curated artwork survive.
- **T5 — Conflicts.** Disagreements are surfaced and never auto-applied.
- **T6 — No plugin write path.** A plugin cannot reach the store except through the review pipeline. Asserted structurally, not by convention.
- **T7 — Credential handling.** Credentials land in Keychain and are removed on uninstall.
- **T8 — Cache replay.** A cached response satisfies a repeat request with no network.
- **T9 — Second-provider drop-in.** Registering a second test provider requires no core change.
- **T10 — Public repository names no plugin.** An automated check greps tracked files for plugin module names, package paths and source names, and fails on any match. Covers `Package.swift`, project files and xcconfigs, not just Swift sources.
- **T11 — Default build is local-only.** The build produced from the public repository alone links no plugin and issues no plugin network request under any code path.
Golden fixtures use recorded responses. No live network in tests.
## Open decisions — Human Operator
- ❓ **Tags from plugins.** May a plugin propose tags? Proposal: yes, treated as any other proposed field in the review sheet, never applied silently.
- ❓ **Batch enrichment.** In-app *enrich all* or per-item only? Proposal: per-item for v1. Bulk stays with the external CSV path, which already has a dry-run change matrix.
- ❓ **Conflict default.** When target and source disagree and the user takes no action — skip, or keep prompting? Proposal: skip and log.
- ❓ **Provider precedence.** With two plugins enriching the same entity type, is there an ordering, or is it always an explicit per-action choice? Proposal: explicit choice, no precedence, until a reason to add one appears.
